thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: Luck plays a far greater role in our lives than we re­alise.
thought.who: Amit Varma, distilling his years at the poker table into a lesson for life

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on poker, cricket and luck
lead.head: Don’t judge the shot by the six

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 19

body: Amit Varma was man­ag­ing ed­i­tor at Cricinfo and trav­elled with the cricket team be­fore spend­ing five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player. Only at the poker table, he said, did he un­der­stand cricket “for what it was”.
What poker taught him was ex­pected value. With Ajay Shah, he ap­plied it to cricket, and then to life it­self.
Varma began with a fair coin. Heads, he pays you 51 paise; tails, you pay him 49. Over a hun­dred flips you should ex­pect a rupee: one paisa a flip.
Take the bet, he said. Yet one flip loses half the time, and on­look­ers will call it a blun­der. Even a hun­dred flips can leave you be­hind.
Shah had a phrase for this. “I al­ways like to say, don’t judge a pol­icy by an out­come.” Many a de­ci­sion, he said, goes wrong “be­cause of dumb luck”. {019-C01}
## Luck, not ge­nius

Poker showed Varma how big luck is. Play Nadal at ten­nis a hun­dred times and you lose every game. The world’s best poker player against a be­gin­ner is closer to 51-49 a hand: skill needs a long sam­ple to show. {019-C03}

“Luck plays a far greater role in our lives than we re­alise,” he said. Good luck, like where you were born, can make you ar­ro­gant; bad luck can make you de­featist. Sweat only what you can con­trol.
Shah said this runs “ex­actly op­po­site to the great man the­ory”: the ad­mired CEO may just have been in soft­ware in the right years.
## The new gram­mar

Then the hosts turned to cricket. A bats­man skies the ball. If it goes for six he is brave; if he is caught he has let his coun­try down. Varma’s point: the out­come alone can­not tell you if the shot was right.
T20, he ar­gued, changed the game “in a very fun­da­men­tal way, and no one no­ticed”: a one-day side has 11 re­sources for 50 overs, a T20 side the same 11 for 20.
With de­liv­er­ies scarce, “the cost of a dot ball, a ball of which no run is scored, is much higher, and the value of a wicket is lower”. Aggression is worth more. {019-C06}
Teams none­the­less brought over the one-day gram­mar: pinch-hit, con­sol­i­date, slog. Varma’s an­swer, first set out in 2014, was to front-load: at­tack all the way and send the hit­ters in first.
A side that fin­ished only two or three wick­ets down, what­ever its score, had not been ag­gres­sive enough. “You left money on the table,” Shah said.

Varma also pro­posed a new yard­stick: a batsman’s strike rate minus the rate his team needed to reach par. If it is neg­a­tive, “the more runs he makes, the greater the li­a­bil­ity he is to his team”. {019-C07}
## Easy on the judg­ment
Aggressive cricket, Varma added, is not al­ways ag­gres­sive bat­ting: fac­ing an im­pos­si­ble tar­get in Delhi in 2015, South Africa’s bats­men barely tried to score, and he thought them right.

His plea to fans: don’t rush to judg­ment. The prob­a­bilis­tic lens, he said, makes bet­ter fans and bet­ter lives: “we can stop being hard on our­selves for things that go wrong, and we can stop judg­ing oth­ers all the time”.
He signed off by telling view­ers that they had taken a gam­ble on the episode, and that by reach­ing the end they had shown “that the gam­ble was worth it”.

second.label: The coin toss
second.head: Heads you win, barely
second.deck: Ajay Shah on John von Neumann, and the edge hidden in a coin toss

pic.caption: John von Neumann, mathematician and physicist

body: A coin toss is sup­posed to be the purest 50-50 there is. Ajay Shah is not so sure.

When Einstein and oth­ers were de­bat­ing prob­a­bil­ity in physics, the math­e­ma­ti­cian John von Neumann, “Johnny to all his good friends”, asked whether a coin toss was truly ran­dom or merely “our fail­ure to com­pute”. {019-S05} Given some ini­tial facts about a coin, his for­mu­las pre­dicted the out­come at about 0.66 to 0.33.

More re­cently, Shah re­called, re­searchers in a global project, which he thought was led by Persi Diaconis, tossed phys­i­cal coins mil­lions of times. A coin start­ing heads-up landed heads about 51 per cent of the time. Shah’s ad­vice: to cheat at an im­por­tant life de­ci­sion, offer a coin toss. {019-J05}

quote.text: is the ran­dom­ness of a coin toss some­thing truly ran­dom about the world, or it is our fail­ure to com­pute?

third.head: Every career is a punt

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on steel or software

body: You may think your­self too risk-averse ever to trade in the stock mar­ket. Ajay Shah’s reply: you are al­ready spec­u­lat­ing with your big­gest asset. {019-S07}

Leaving col­lege, Shah would put a ques­tion to peo­ple his age. Suppose you bought shares in a few in­dus­tries for 30 years, bet­ting on whether steel or soft­ware would do well. Everyone agreed that was spec­u­la­tive.

Yet choos­ing an in­dus­try or a work­place, he said, is the same bet, made with your human cap­i­tal, an asset you can­not di­ver­sify. In the 1980s, who could have known that Indian pharma, or Indian soft­ware, would do so well? {#pharma}
By dumb luck, some peo­ple chose those ca­reers and now look great. The media li­onises them as ge­niuses. “Actually,” Shah said, “it is just the forces of luck in our life.”

p2.title: Think like a gambler
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on judging the decision, not the outcome, from the coin toss to the crease {019-C01}

from1.head: Don’t judge the shot by the six

quote.text: After some­thing has hap­pened, it has hun­dred per­cent hap­pened or zero per­cent hap­pened. But be­fore any­thing hap­pens, it is prob­a­bilis­tic.

box.title: The columns behind the episode
box.text: Amit Varma made the case in two pieces in 2016, *What Cricket Can Learn From Poker* and *What Cricket Can Learn From Economics*: one brings ex­pected value to the game, the other op­por­tu­nity cost. {019-R04}

sections.label: Expected value
sections.head: Right call, wrong outcome
sections.caption: expected value
body: Geeks, Amit Varma said, will call a de­ci­sion “plus EV”. To ex­plain what that means, he began not with cricket but with a coin, and promised to bring in Asimov and Clarke.
If some­one of­fers you 51 paise for every heads and asks for 49 for every tails, ac­cept. Your ex­pected value is one paisa a throw. {#ev}
But the world judges by re­sults. Lose one flip and peo­ple will point at you: “What a bad de­ci­sion. You made such a blun­der.”
## A uni­verse for every flip

Here came the sci­ence fic­tion. Every flip, Varma said, splits the world into two par­al­lel uni­verses, heads and tails, and each splits again. Somewhere there is a uni­verse with a hun­dred heads in a row. Which one you land in is pure luck.
So you can­not eval­u­ate what you do by how it worked out, he ar­gued; you can only live by a good set of rules. {019-C02}

Poker runs on the same sums. Facing an all-in of 100 ru­pees into a pot of 100, a player with a flush draw needs to win a third of the time just to break even. Add a gut­shot straight draw and his chances rise to 42 per cent; now the call pays. {#flush}
~ So poker play­ers are taught not to be re­sults-oriented, Varma said. Ajay Shah’s ver­sion was shorter: don’t judge a pol­icy by an out­come.

quote.text: After some­thing has hap­pened, it has hun­dred per­cent hap­pened or zero per­cent hap­pened. But be­fore any­thing hap­pens, it is prob­a­bilis­tic.

sections.label: Speculation
sections.head: Life above the API
sections.caption: life above the API
body: In po­lite com­pany in India, Ajay Shah said, wise, sta­ble, grown-up peo­ple are not sup­posed to spec­u­late. He wants to re­ha­bil­i­tate the word.

Anything sig­nif­i­cant, he ar­gued, in­volves judg­ment under un­cer­tainty: a sur­geon on a di­ag­nos­tic path­way, a fi­nancier choos­ing where to put money, the two hosts de­cid­ing whether to build a new YouTube show. A worker on an as­sem­bly line, by con­trast, lives a non-speculative life.
“If you wish to ban­ish spec­u­la­tion from your life,” he said, “then you prob­a­bly want a very dull life.” {019-C04}

Amit Varma had made a sim­i­lar point ear­lier, cit­ing his col­umn *We Are All Gamblers*: choos­ing be­tween real es­tate and other in­vest­ments, or be­tween soft­ware and tele­vi­sion, is an im­plicit bet. {019-R09}
## Above and below
Shah then di­vided the world into those who live above the API and those who live below it. An Uber driver is told by code to take this cus­tomer from here to there. He has no agency. {019-C05}
Varma, risk­ing ex­pul­sion from Shah’s cir­cle of friends, asked bluntly what an API was. {019-J06}

An ap­pli­ca­tion pro­gram­ming in­ter­face, Shah ex­plained: a func­tion that takes an in­struc­tion and re­turns a pre­dictable an­swer “time after time after time”. The de­sign­ing, de­cid­ing and risk-taking hap­pen above it.
~ “And we should all be above the API,” Varma said. Shah agreed, adding: “Most of us aren’t.”

quote.text: There are the peo­ple in the world who live above the API, and there are the peo­ple who live below the API.

art.caption: Amit Varma (right) on life above the API, with Ajay Shah

sections.label: The skied shot
sections.head: Caught, or just unlucky?
sections.caption: the skied shot
body: As a cricket writer and ed­i­tor, Amit Varma found writ­ers and fans alike “too quick to pass judg­ment”.

Take a bats­man who, at a cru­cial mo­ment, tries to hit a six and skies it. Varma of­fered three out­comes: a six, a catch in the out­field, or a ball that hits a bird, falls on a fielder’s head and kills them both. The last, he al­lowed, is “in­cred­i­bly un­likely”. {019-J07}
Caught, he is ir­re­spon­si­ble; six, he is the brave hit­ter who res­cued his side. Either way, Varma said, the re­sult is no ver­dict on the de­ci­sion.
## What foot­ball knows
Other sports have bro­ken this down to a sci­ence. Football coaches know the ex­pected value of a long shot against a pass to the striker, and drill it into their play­ers.

When Pep Guardiola came to Manchester City, Varma said, he got rid of a goal­keeper good enough to play for England, be­cause he could not play out from the back. {019-S06} Sometimes that style gifts the op­po­nent the ball. “But on the whole it is plus EV.”
~ Cricket lacked such data, Varma ar­gued, be­cause al­most every Test sit­u­a­tion, such as a fourth-day dust bowl at Motera, is unique. The stan­dard­ised T20 for­mat changed that.

quote.text: this whole logic of play out from the back can look ridicu­lous, when you end up giv­ing the ball away with a bad pass.

sections.label: Twenty overs
sections.head: Scarce balls, cheap wickets
sections.caption: the cost of a dot ball
body: In one-day cricket a side has 11 re­sources for 50 overs; in T20, the same 11 for 20. Amit Varma ap­plied op­por­tu­nity cost: with de­liv­er­ies scarcer, a dot ball costs more and a wicket less. {019-C06}

That up­ends the old sta­tis­tics. Averages and ag­gre­gates no longer mat­ter, Varma said; strike rate does. A bats­man who makes 900 runs in an IPL sea­son, slower than his team needed, was “ac­tu­ally a dis­as­ter”. {#ninehundred}
Ajay Shah called this “the quin­tes­sen­tial prob­lem of all or­gan­i­sa­tions”: a player’s urge to look good pulls against the team’s need to win.
## The hur­dle rate
Judge bats­men by av­er­ages, Shah said, and you set them on the wrong tra­jec­tory. Judge them against a hur­dle rate: what it takes to win.
The fix must go up­stream to the se­lec­tors, Shah said: “It is pos­si­ble to re­cruit a star trader in a dumb way, and it is the fault of the man­age­ment that hired those star traders.” {019-C08}
Selectors, Varma added, often come from an older school, and find it safer to pick a man with a good av­er­age than one who cor­rectly risks his wicket and gets un­lucky.
~ The sums also shift dur­ing a match. Lose three wick­ets in the first over, Varma said, and the re­main­ing wick­ets gain in value, so cau­tion is worth more.

quote.text: It would have been bet­ter if he lasted two balls in each in­nings and didn’t waste time.

sections.label: The forecasters
sections.head: The certainty merchants
sections.caption: selling certainty
body: Amit Varma once planned a book on what poker taught him about think­ing prob­a­bilis­ti­cally. Then he read *Superforecasting*, by Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner, and de­cided his own book was not re­quired. {#tetlock}

The book, he said, teaches the hu­mil­ity to keep up­dat­ing your pri­ors and ex­am­in­ing your bi­ases. Experts on TV and Twitter are in­cen­tivised to exude cer­tainty, but in a com­plex world cer­tainty is hard to come by.

Ajay Shah, as an econ­o­mist, is con­stantly asked what the stock mar­ket or the ex­change rate will do, and finds it “brac­ing to say, I don’t know”. Understanding fi­nance, he said, means re­spect­ing its un­cer­tainty. {019-C09}
## Seventy, twenty, ten

Pressed for an an­swer, Varma said, an hon­est fore­caster gives prob­a­bil­i­ties: 70 per cent this, 20 per cent that. Those who gave Donald Trump a low chance in 2016 were cas­ti­gated when he won, but they did not nec­es­sar­ily get it wrong. {#trump}
Shah finds the con­ver­sa­tion be­tween econ­o­mists and the real world in India “a bit dys­func­tional”, be­cause peo­ple want a super-forecaster. Better, he said, to talk about the forces at work.
~ He re­called Churchill’s lament: one econ­o­mist gives you two views, “and three if it’s John Maynard Keynes”. {019-J12}
~ Shah’s own pick, *Thinking Strategically* by Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff, takes game the­ory in the sense of John von Neumann closer to real-world use. {#dixit}

quote.text: Understanding fi­nance is learn­ing to re­spect the un­cer­tainty of that beast.

There is a uni­verse of pos­si­bil­i­ties. There are so many par­al­lel uni­verses about to split up with every de­ci­sion that you make. So you can­not eval­u­ate any­thing that you do on the basis of how it worked out.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A bookshop, a betting tip, a Delhi rearguard and the long road to Bazball

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s betting tip, and why it worked so well
stories.head: The tip that called 13 of 14
body: By 2016 Amit Varma had re­tired from poker, but many poker play­ers he knew dab­bled in cricket bet­ting. He says he never has, and does not ad­vise it: “It is il­le­gal in India, so kindly, gen­tle reader, don’t do it.”
Before that year’s IPL, one such friend came to him for a tip. Surely a man who un­der­stood cricket so well could see an edge.
Varma’s ad­vice was a sin­gle line: al­ways bet on the side bat­ting sec­ond, what­ever the price. The friend had ex­pected some­thing deep and nu­anced. He ig­nored it. {019-S02}

After the 14th match he rang back. Had he lis­tened, Varma told him, he would have made a lot of money. The chas­ing side had won 13 of the 14, eas­ily, los­ing 3.4 wick­ets on av­er­age and fin­ish­ing in around 17 overs. {#thirteen}

Chasing does carry a small edge, Varma said, be­cause the side bat­ting sec­ond knows ex­actly what it needs. But that is worth 55-45, or 60-40 at most. “Why was there this mas­sive skew? Because teams were un­der­es­ti­mat­ing the par score.” {#skew}

The par score is the one that wins about half the time. Virat Kohli, then cap­tain­ing Bangalore, lost at least three games in that run after bat­ting first, Varma re­called, and im­plic­itly blamed his bowlers: “we got the par score”. By Varma’s reck­on­ing, they had fallen well short.
~ Teams were still think­ing in an older par­a­digm, he said. That has since sig­nif­i­cantly cor­rected it­self, “be­cause ob­vi­ously you live and learn”, but some still make the same er­rors.
stories.why: When the rules of a game change, play­ers keep using the old men­tal model. That hands a big, sys­tem­atic edge to any­one who has up­dated, enough for a one-line tip to beat any amount of nu­ance.
stories.postscript: Varma had writ­ten count­less col­umns over ten years on T20’s changed gram­mar. They were, he said, “all com­pletely ig­nored”. {#tenyears}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the side batting second

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s first poker column, and a lesson in nerve
stories.head: Fortune favours the bookworm
body: Amit Varma once wrote a poker col­umn for the *Economic Times* called *Range Rover*. The first in­stal­ment was *The Bookshop Romeo*. {019-R10}
A young man whose favourite au­thor is Milan Kundera walks into a book­shop. In a dis­tant aisle he sees a pretty girl read­ing Kundera. Should he go up and in­tro­duce him­self?

Suppose he is dif­fi­dent, Varma said, and puts the chance of a date at 10 per cent and of a soul­mate at 1 per cent. Those out­comes are worth so much, and a re­jec­tion costs so lit­tle, that the ap­proach is “mas­sively plus EV”. {019-S01}
~ Nobody in a book­shop ac­tu­ally does the sum. “You just in­tu­itively know that I have noth­ing to lose,” Varma said, and the logic ap­plies to every part of life, cricket in­cluded.
stories.why: Expected value is not only for gam­blers. When the down­side is a moment’s em­bar­rass­ment and the up­side a soul­mate, the shot is worth tak­ing every time, and nam­ing the sum stops fear pass­ing it­self off as pru­dence.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Bookshop Romeo

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the day two stroke-players stopped scoring
stories.head: Dead bat, live brain
body: On 6 December 2015, the fourth day of a Test in Delhi, South Africa went in need­ing about 431 runs to beat India, with a day and a half left. {#delhi}

They judged a win im­pos­si­ble on that pitch against those bowlers, Amit Varma said, so risk brought no re­ward. “Over here, there is no cost to a dot ball, and the value of a wicket is in­fi­nite.” {019-S03}
So Hashim Amla made 25 runs in about 244 balls, and AB de Villiers, one of the most ag­gres­sive bats­men of all time, made 43 in about 293. {#amla}

~ Onlookers could not be­lieve nat­u­ral stroke-players were bat­ting like this. To Varma, they had cal­cu­lated the ex­pected value and done the right thing for their team, “even if it looked stupid”.
stories.why: Aggressive cricket is not al­ways ag­gres­sive bat­ting. The logic that de­mands at­tack in T20 de­mands total de­fence when risk earns noth­ing, and the right call can look fool­ish to an au­di­ence that judges by style.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Amla and de Villiers

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how cricket learnt to attack, slowly
stories.head: From 36 not out to Bazball
body: When one-day cricket ar­rived, teams played it like Tests, Amit Varma said. In the ’75 World Cup, Sunil Gavaskar bat­ted all 60 overs for 36 not out. His de­fence: he didn’t play every ball. {#gavaskar}

Varma re­called New Zealand send­ing Mark Greatbatch in as a pinch-hitter at the ’91 World Cup, and Jayasuriya and Kaluwitharana at­tack­ing from the start in ’96. The mid­dle overs stayed for con­sol­i­da­tion. {#greatbatch}

About seven or eight years ago England began front-loading in ODIs. Scores of 300-plus be­came reg­u­lar out­side the sub­con­ti­nent. {#threehundred} In 2019 they won the World Cup, with some luck in the final. {019-S04}

~ Under coach Brendan McCullum, known as Baz, they took this into Tests. Varma’s for­mer Cricinfo col­league Andrew Miller coined “Bazball”; McCullum dis­likes it: “It’s not just all crash and burn.” England’s real edge, Varma said, was ex­pected value.

quote.text: they were the first to recog­nise that the ODI game for the last three decades had ac­tu­ally been played wrong.

quiz.q: What is Ajay Shah’s pithy rule for judging decisions made under uncertainty?
quiz.a: Don’t judge a pol­icy by an out­come; judge it by ex­pected value.

quiz.q: What did John von Neumann wonder about the randomness of a coin toss?
quiz.a: Whether it was truly ran­dom or merely our fail­ure to com­pute.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s example, who lives below the API, and what does he lack?
quiz.a: The Uber driver, told by code where to take each cus­tomer; he has no agency.

quiz.q: Why does T20, by Amit Varma’s reasoning, make dot balls costlier and wickets cheaper?
quiz.a: The same 11 re­sources are spread over 20 overs in­stead of 50.

quiz.q: What one-line betting tip did Varma give a friend before the 2016 IPL?
quiz.a: Always bet on the side bat­ting sec­ond, what­ever the price.

quiz.q: Why did Pep Guardiola get rid of a goalkeeper good enough for England?
quiz.a: He couldn’t play out from the back, which Guardiola’s ap­proach de­manded.

glossary.def: Having pos­i­tive ex­pected value: worth doing on av­er­age, what­ever hap­pens.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 19. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Hashim Amla (YellowMonkey/Blnguyen, CC BY-SA 4.0); John von Neumann (Wikimedia Commons, Attribution); Avinash Dixit (Wikimedia Commons, Copyrighted free use).

shelf.title: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
shelf.creator: Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner
shelf.why: A mas­ter­ful primer on prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing: TV ex­perts, re­warded for ex­ud­ing cer­tainty, are often wrong, while good fore­cast­ers keep up­dat­ing their pri­ors.

shelf.title: Thinking Strategically: The Competitive Edge in Business, Politics, and Everyday Life
shelf.creator: Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff
shelf.why: Draws on game the­ory (‘strategically’ in the sense of John von Neumann) and brings that body of knowl­edge close to real-world ap­pli­ca­tions.

shelf.title: A First Course in Probability
shelf.creator: Sheldon Ross
shelf.why: The clas­sic prob­a­bil­ity text­book be­hind the episode’s ex­pected-value rea­son­ing, for any­one who wants the rig­or­ous maths be­neath the in­tu­itions.

shelf.title: What Cricket Can Learn From Poker
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s foun­da­tional case for ap­ply­ing ex­pected value and prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing to cricket, with foot­ball data show­ing how far other sports had al­ready moved.

shelf.title: What Cricket Can Learn From Economics
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Applies the economist’s idea of op­por­tu­nity cost to cricket.

shelf.title: Resources vs Constraints - Why T20 Teams Need to Attack More
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Sets out the core T20 ar­gu­ment of the episode: the same 11 re­sources spread over only 20 overs means teams should at­tack far more than they do.

shelf.title: The lesson from this IPL: Front-load your innings
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s orig­i­nal ar­gu­ment that T20 teams should drop the pinch-consolidate-slog gram­mar in­her­ited from ODIs: send the hit­ters in first, keep at­tack­ing for all twenty overs and hold the an­chor back for emer­gen­cies.

shelf.title: Unlikely is Inevitable
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s col­umn on the law of truly large num­bers: with a big enough sam­ple, un­likely runs are bound to hap­pen, so los­ing sev­eral hands in a row as an 80% favourite is nei­ther a rigged game nor proof of a bad de­ci­sion, and bad luck shouldn’t be read as fate.

shelf.title: We Are All Gamblers
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that every life choice, from mar­riage to jobs to stocks, is a bet weighed on prob­a­bil­i­ties, so ‘gambler’ shouldn’t be an in­sult and sin­gling out gam­bling for stigma makes lit­tle sense.

shelf.title: The Bookshop Romeo
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s col­umn with the Milan Kundera book­shop ex­am­ple: a high-reward, near-zero-cost move is mas­sively plus-EV, a por­ta­ble il­lus­tra­tion of ex­pected value in ev­ery­day life.

shelf.title: Range Rover (archive of Amit’s poker column)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The ar­chive of the poker col­umn Amit wrote for the Economic Times, in which he ap­plied poker’s prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing be­yond the table: the full body of his poker writ­ing for read­ers who want to go deeper.

shelf.title: Luck is All Around
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A short, vivid case for how much luck lies be­hind your ex­is­tence and ev­ery­thing else, and the life les­son that fol­lows: don’t let good luck make you ar­ro­gant or bad luck make you de­featist.

shelf.title: Om Namah Volume
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: One of Amit’s poker col­umns, on his life les­son to ‘put in volume’: a small edge pays off only over a large sam­ple.

shelf.title: Never Mind the Bullocks, Here’s the Lamborghini
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Part of Amit’s decade-long, often ig­nored cam­paign ar­gu­ing that T20 had fun­da­men­tally changed how the game should be played.

shelf.title: The New Face of Cricket
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: For read­ers who want more of his ar­gu­ment that the game’s gram­mar had changed while most teams hadn’t no­ticed.

shelf.title: National Highway 420 (and the EV of Aggressive Batting)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s col­umn ap­ply­ing ex­pected value to cricket: ag­gres­sive bat­ting pays, and teams bat­ting first were sys­tem­at­i­cally un­der­es­ti­mat­ing the par score.

shelf.title: The Winning Mantra for this IPL: Attack, Attack, Attack
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Another in­stal­ment of his ar­gu­ment that the EV of ag­gres­sion in T20 is far higher than teams as­sume.

shelf.title: For this Brave New World of cricket, we have IPL and England to thank
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Celebrates England as the first team to re­alise ODI cricket had been played too con­ser­va­tively for three decades.

shelf.title: Poker and Stock Markets (Episode 47 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Mohit Satyanand
shelf.why: Mohit Satyanand on the cog­ni­tive bi­ases poker and in­vest­ing share, and on poker-style prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing ap­plied to mar­kets.

shelf.title: Fair coins tend to land on the same side they started
shelf.creator: František Bartoš et al.
shelf.why: The em­pir­i­cal basis for the find­ing that a coin tossed heads-up lands heads about 51% of the time, show­ing struc­ture hid­den in­side ap­par­ent ran­dom­ness.

shelf.title: eventstudies (open-source R package)
shelf.creator: XKDR Forum
shelf.why: An event study could mea­sure whether a six shifts ex­pected runs or wicket prob­a­bil­ity over the next few balls.

laughs.text: Ajay’s im­pro­vised intro paints Amit as a ‘se­ri­ous philosopher’ who spends his nights read­ing com­plex books by German philoso­phers. Amit: ‘I did, I con­fess, read German philoso­phers, but that is not some­thing that one ad­mits in pub­lic.’ The show notes title the chap­ter ‘What? He Reads German Philosophers? Scoundrel!’
Ajay on von Neumann: ‘Johnny to all his good friends. There’s only one Johnny in the world, and that’s Johnny von Neumann.’

Ajay’s prac­ti­cal take­away from the 51% coin-toss find­ing: ‘when­ever you want to cheat at im­por­tant life de­ci­sions, offer to the blokes around you, let’s toss the coin, and I’ve given you a slight edge.’

After Ajay’s lec­ture on liv­ing above the API, Amit asks: ‘I might get kicked out from your cir­cle of friends for ask­ing this ques­tion, but I have to. On be­half of our gen­tle lis­ten­ers as well. What the fuck is an API?’
Ajay: ‘now shut up and give us cricket.’ Amit: ‘I can’t shut up and give you cricket, I have to talk.’

Ajay re­calls watch­ing Sunil Gavaskar bat at Wankhede as a child and says Sachin Tendulkar grew up about fifty me­tres from him in Bandra East. Amit: ‘A day should come when Sachin Tendulkar says, You know, I grew up in the same neigh­bor­hood as Ajay Shah. I would like that day to come.’

Amit’s sign-off to the au­di­ence: ‘you were tak­ing a gam­ble when you started watch­ing this episode. But it is very clear now that you have reached the end, that the gam­ble was worth it. So con­grat­u­la­tions.’
Amit spec­i­fies a per­fectly fair coin, ‘not like the Sholay coin, but a proper legit coin’, a nod to the fa­mous coin in the film Sholay.
Amit prom­ises to bring Asimov and Clarke into a prob­a­bil­ity les­son, ex­plain­ing ex­pected value through sci­ence-fictional par­al­lel uni­verses that split with every coin flip.

‘Bazball’, coined by Andrew Miller, Amit’s ex-colleague at Cricinfo, after England coach Brendan ‘Baz’ McCullum. McCullum hates the label: ‘I don’t re­ally like that silly term... It’s not just all crash and burn.’

Harry Truman’s plea for ‘a one-handed economist’, made be­cause his ad­vis­ers kept say­ing ‘on one hand this, on the other hand that.’ Amit sym­pa­thises with both Truman, who had to de­cide, and the econ­o­mists, be­cause the world is not sim­ple.
Ajay re­calls Churchill’s lament that one econ­o­mist gives you two views, ‘and three if it’s John Maynard Keynes.’
